title: What Does a Construction Cost Estimate Include? 2026 Guide
desc: What a construction cost estimate covers under the Construction Law 2025 and Decree 206/2026: construction, equipment, consulting, contingency.
summary: The items in a construction cost estimate under the Construction Law 2025 and Decree 206/2026/ND-CP, and how homeowners can use an estimate to control the cost of building a house.
body: Before signing a construction contract, a homeowner should have a clear cost estimate. This article summarizes what a construction estimate includes under Article 76 of the Construction Law 2025 and Decree 206/2026/ND-CP on construction investment cost management (effective 1 July 2026, replacing Decree 10/2021/ND-CP).
1. What is a construction cost estimate?

A construction cost estimate is the projected cost of building a work, performing a bid package, or carrying out a construction task. There are three kinds: the estimate for a construction work, for a bid package, and for a task; the investor decides which to prepare as appropriate (Clauses 1, 3, 4 and 5, Article 76). A work estimate is prepared on the basis of the construction design, so the estimate is only close to reality when full drawings exist.
2. Must a private house follow Decree 206?

Decree 206/2026/ND-CP is mandatory for public investment projects, PPP projects, and projects using state budget funds. Organizations and individuals with other projects, such as a household's house, may use it as a reference to determine and manage costs and are responsible for their own decisions (Article 2). Even so, the way the decree divides cost items is an excellent framework for reading and comparing quotations.
3. The six cost groups in a work estimate
Under Point a, Clause 2, Article 76, a construction work estimate includes:
Equipment costs (if any): the cost of purchasing building equipment and technology equipment and related costs (Clause 3, Article 12).
Construction consulting costs: the cost of construction investment consulting tasks from the preparation stage to the end of construction (Article 26).
Under Clause 2, Article 12 of Decree 206/2026/ND-CP, construction costs include:
Direct costs: materials, labor, and construction machinery and equipment, calculated as the design quantity multiplied by the corresponding construction price;
Indirect costs: overhead and the cost of certain tasks whose quantities cannot be determined from the design;
Pre-calculated taxable income, determined by a percentage norm as prescribed;
Temporary housing costs for living quarters and site management.
5. Contingency: the item most often forgotten

Contingency has two parts: a contingency for additional quantities and work and a contingency for price escalation, calculated as a percentage of the total costs. The escalation rate is determined by the construction period and the construction price index for the type of work (Clause 7, Article 12). The provincial construction price index is determined by the Department of Construction for the provincial People's Committee to announce (Article 23).
6. Where do the prices used in an estimate come from?

Estimates may refer to and use the system of norms and construction prices, equipment prices, and price indices announced by state authorities, or market prices, manufacturer quotations, and data from similar works (Clause 1, Article 12; Article 19, Article 22).
Require an estimate with quantities taken off from the drawings, stating the material types clearly; avoid quotations that give only a price per m² of floor area.
Check that all six cost groups are present, especially consulting costs and contingency.

An estimate is different from the contract price: this decree does not regulate contract prices, payment, or final settlement (Clause 2, Article 1); those matters must be stated clearly in the construction contract.

This article is a summary for reference only and does not replace legal documents. Decree 206/2026/ND-CP is mandatory for projects using state funds and PPP projects; for private houses it is for reference only. For detailed norms and methods, see also the Ministry of Construction's Circulars guiding cost management.
